{"id": "11:84/q16", "question": "What is the 'good' in which Shuʿayb sees them?", "turns_on": "The notes range from prices or material abundance to divine guidance or Shuʿayb's goodwill.", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q16/p1", "position": "Ample wealth, provision, blessing, and worldly prosperity.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī prefers a broad worldly sense embracing adornment, low prices and wealth; Ibn Zayd cites 2:180 for wealth as khayr. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers wealth because it makes fraud indefensible. Qatāda says visible luxury; Wāḥidī mentions fertility; Rāzī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī also connect it to adequate resources."}, {"id": "11:84/q16/p2", "position": "Low or favorable prices.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan are repeatedly cited; Ibn al-Jawzī's lexical note gives this sense. Al-Farrāʾ combines cheap prices with wealth, arguing fraud is needless."}, {"id": "11:84/q16/p3", "position": "Fertile conditions, abundant crops and earnings.", "reasons": "Mujāhid is cited for fertility; Māwardī adds crops and earnings."}, {"id": "11:84/q16/p4", "position": "God's favor can include reason, guidance and provision.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this removes excuse for both idolatry and corrupt dealings; Sūlamī relates favor to the danger of failing gratitude. Qāshānī gives an inward reading of preparedness for perfection and guidance despite vice."}, {"id": "11:84/q16/p5", "position": "Shuʿayb looks on them with goodwill and desires their happiness.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the following warning explains his benevolent concern."}]}
{"id": "11:84/q17", "question": "Why mention their present good before warning them?", "turns_on": "The good can remove need for fraud, call for gratitude, or be a state that fraud will destroy.", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q17/p1", "position": "Prosperity removes any need to cheat.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Rāzī, Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Biqāʿī, Bursevī and Ibn ʿĀshūr make this inference; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it one of two deterrents."}, {"id": "11:84/q17/p2", "position": "Blessing calls for gratitude, generosity, justice and better conduct.", "reasons": "Sūlamī fears falling short in gratitude; Zamakhsharī, Bayḍāwī, Ālūsī and Elmalılı urge good conduct. Ibn ʿĀshūr says Shuʿayb presents himself as witness to God's favor; Islahi says ingratitude can turn luxury to destruction."}, {"id": "11:84/q17/p3", "position": "Wrongdoing could destroy their current good.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī compares the believing man's words in 40:29. Wāḥidī, Baghawī and Rāzī warn of lost blessing and rising prices unless they repent."}]}
{"id": "11:84/q18", "question": "What does Shuʿayb mean by 'I fear'?", "turns_on": "Whether the threatened event is known as certain or depends on continued wrongdoing.", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q18/p1", "position": "He genuinely fears it, since repentance may avert it.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports the alternative: they may quit fraud out of fear, so expectation rather than certain knowledge is appropriate. Elmalılı emphasizes compassion."}, {"id": "11:84/q18/p2", "position": "He means 'I know' that punishment will occur.", "reasons": "Rāzī transmits this from Ibn ʿAbbās."}]}
{"id": "11:84/q19", "question": "Which punishment is the 'encompassing day'?", "turns_on": "Whether the warning names price rises, worldly destruction, the afterlife, or an inclusive threat.", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q19/p1", "position": "Worldly destruction that overtakes all of them.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Māwardī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Rāzī and Qurṭubī give this reading; Biqāʿī says it reaches young, old, and property. Ṭabāṭabāʾī relates the later cloud, cry and earthquake and salvation of believers."}, {"id": "11:84/q19/p2", "position": "Ruinous high prices, drought, and loss of provision.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās links good low prices to threatened high prices; Mujāhid adds drought and famine. The Prophet is reported to say cheating brings withheld provision or high prices; Ibn Mājah's Ibn ʿUmar report adds hard years and unjust rulers, without grading."}, {"id": "11:84/q19/p3", "position": "The Fire or punishment on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Māwardī and Qurṭubī report the Fire; Rāzī says the Day of Resurrection is appointed for condemned people. Ibn Kathīr takes the afterlife."}, {"id": "11:84/q19/p4", "position": "The threat includes worldly and afterlife punishment, or every kind of punishment.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers the encompassing general sense, comparing a circle and 18:42; Ibn ʿĀshūr leaves both worlds open. Ālūsī notes either Resurrection or annihilation; Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows either and says no escape, helper, repentance or intercession."}]}
{"id": "11:84/q20", "question": "What does muḥīṭ convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q20/p1", "position": "It surrounds and reaches everyone, leaving no escape.", "reasons": "Jishumī likens it to a wall and notes the verb can mean containing with care. Zamakhsharī and Ālūsī invoke the ruined garden of 18:42 and an enemy's siege; Biqāʿī says punishment surrounds every side; the current surrounding blessings give way to surrounding harm."}]}
{"id": "11:84/q21", "question": "Why is the day called encompassing, and how does the adjective attach?", "turns_on": "Whether the day itself figuratively bears its punishment's quality, the adjective attaches by proximity, or a noun is omitted.", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q21/p1", "position": "The adjective grammatically describes the day but figuratively means its punishment encompasses them.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī compares 'a burned garment'; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also allows the day's evil itself surrounding them. Rāzī compares 11:77; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the genitive phrase makes the figure clear."}, {"id": "11:84/q21/p2", "position": "Calling the entire day encompassing intensifies the threat, since it contains every event and torment.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Abū Ḥayyān, Biqāʿī and Ālūsī say this is stronger than an encompassing punishment; Ālūsī says one punishment may reach everyone, but an encompassing day gathers every kind, citing a poetic dome image."}, {"id": "11:84/q21/p3", "position": "Muḥīṭ may modify ʿadhāb through attraction by adjacency.", "reasons": "Samīn reports this analysis; Ālūsī also reports it."}, {"id": "11:84/q21/p4", "position": "Muḥīṭ may describe the day with an omitted reference to 'its punishment'.", "reasons": "Samīn reports this ellipsis; Abū al-Baqāʾ objects that an explicit pronoun would be needed, and Ālūsī rejects it as remote."}]}
{"id": "11:84/q22", "question": "How are the suffix yāʾs in 'I see you' and 'I fear' pronounced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q22/p1", "position": "An added final yāʾ may be opened with fatḥa, without change of meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Bazzī joins the Medinans for wa-innī arākum; Nâshir says the Medinans, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr open yāʾ in three innī akhāf contexts. Qiraat Encyclopedia notes the open suffix in both verse occurrences."}]}
{"id": "11:84/q23", "question": "How does this story connect with nearby prophetic accounts and parallel verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q23/p1", "position": "It continues the sequence of prophetic missions and parallels earlier accounts.", "reasons": "Rāzī calls it the sixth narrative; Biqāʿī links the turn from Lot to the nearest famous story in time. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ālūsī compare the opening with Ṣāliḥ at 11:61; Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Asad and Study Quran point to the parallel in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf and other cited passages."}]}
{"id": "11:84/q24", "question": "What happened to Shuʿayb's people after this warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q24/p1", "position": "Most rejected him, persecuted believers, and were destroyed while he and the believers survived.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 7:86, 7:89, 26:187 and 7:93 for obstruction, threatened expulsion or stoning, his prayer, and cloud, cry and earthquake. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports they challenged the warning; Khalaf says tiny cheating amounts were enough for ruin."}]}
{"id": "11:84/q25", "question": "What conduct toward God and people does the verse teach?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q25/p1", "position": "Monotheism and fair dealing jointly require reform, gratitude, and respect for others' rights.", "reasons": "Asad calls them twin requirements and rejects a merely historical limit. Kuran Yolu says honesty toward people is bound to honesty toward God. Ṭabāṭabāʾī links reciprocal rights and social cooperation; Elmalılı says the account bears on contemporary civilization."}]}
{"id": "11:84/q26", "question": "What inward warning is drawn from their prosperity and threatened punishment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q26/p1", "position": "Ease can conceal spiritual danger; their capacity for guidance may be lost through ingratitude and attachment to gains.", "reasons": "Sūlamī calls security and successive blessings nearest to gradual ensnarement; Qāshānī says vice veils truth and turns people from human to animal perfections. Bursevī depicts injustice hardening and surrounding the heart's mirror."}]}

{"id": "11:87/q02", "question": "What does 'your prayers' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣalāt names his ritual act, religion, recitation, supplication, or place.", "positions": [{"id": "11:87/q02/p1", "position": "Shuayb's ritual prayer or worship.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and al-Ahnaf report his frequent prayer. {"id": "11:87/q03", "question": "Why speak of prayer as commanding?", "turns_on": "Hostile ridicule, figurative moral effect, or affirmative answer.", "positions": [{"id": "11:87/q03/p1", "position": "They ridicule his frequent devotion and its moral authority.", "reasons": "Several commentators say they winked and laughed as he prayed. Their taunt portrays the call as delusion."}, {"id": "11:87/q03/p2", "position": "Prayer figuratively commands by urging right conduct.", "reasons": "Sahib al-Nazm, al-Zamakhshari and others invoke 29:45; prayer is part of faith that restrains wrongdoing."}, {"id": "11:87/q03/p3", "position": "Prayer really did enjoin abandoning idols.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan answers the people's question affirmatively."}]}
{"id": "11:87/q04", "question": "How can prayer command Shuayb concerning their action?", "turns_on": "Whether a complement is omitted or the awkward attribution is intentional.", "positions": [{"id": "11:87/q04/p1", "position": "An omitted term means it moves Shuayb to command or charge them.", "reasons": "Sahib al-Nazm supplies a repeated command; al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan supply a charge because one person cannot perform another's act. Al-Alusi reports omitted taklif and preposition."}, {"id": "11:87/q04/p2", "position": "Direct attribution to prayer is itself part of the taunt.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai locates mockery in assigning the command to prayer; al-Alusi considers a reading without ellipsis but objects to its contextual motivation."}]}

{"id": "11:87/q06", "question": "Why is their fathers' worship in present tense?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:87/q06/p1", "position": "It expresses dead ancestors' past practice in present form.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi compares 2:102."}]}

{"id": "11:87/q08", "question": "How does 'or that we do' attach?", "turns_on": "The verb persons, an omitted prohibition, and whether the received reading would command fraud.", "positions": [{"id": "11:87/q08/p1", "position": "It coordinates with what the fathers worship: leave worship and chosen wealth practices.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari's Basrans, al-Nahhas, al-Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Samin and Ibn Hisham give this parse.
